newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-INL sees profit up in '98 depite Sky buy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-INL sees profit up in '98 depite Sky buy.

text.p: New Zealand publisher Independent Newspapers Ltd, controlled by media baron Ruert Murdoch, expects to raise its net profit in 1997/98 despite plans to purchase a stake in loss-making Sky Network Television, managing director Mike Robson said on Friday.
INL earlier reported a net profit of NZ$50.42 million for the year to June 30 1997, up from $47.18 million last year.
"We think we'll be better than the $50 million," Robson said of the 1998 year profit.

"It's a bit hard to say because the trading climate at the moment is pretty indifferent. But because of the large charge against the business this year in non-trading items, we're liable to have a better run at it next year," he told Reuters in an interview.
Abnormal costs after tax amounted to $8.7 million in the 1997 year and Robson said he did not expect INL to incur a similar amount of one-off costs this financial year.

"There will be some, but we're certainly not going to have another write-off of the (CD-Rom) Teramedia business, we're not going to have a major restructuring of (magazine distributor) Gordon and Gotch in Australia again," he said.

"Some of the other accounting adjustments we wouldn't expect to see again either, so there's a large portion of abnormal costs there and that's why we're reasonably confident that we will be able to beat the net profit, notwithstanding a pretty lousy trading environment at the moment."
Robson said his profit forecast took all the implications of the planned Sky purchase into account.
Sky is a New Zealand pay television operator unrelated to the Sky satellite television firms controlled by Murdoch.
INL is currently in negotiations to buy the 51 percent of Sky held by HKP Partners, a United States consortium owned by Bell Atlantic, Ameritech, TCI Communications and Time Warner.

It is INL's second attempt at securing a piece of Sky after protracted talks broke down in February this year. Robson said he was not concerned that the company's negotiations with HKP Partners were also proving to be a drawn out affair.
"We're in negotiations and we're reasonably satisfied but we'll make an announcement on that when we've completed them," he said, adding he expected a resolution "shortly".
Analysts are forecasting a net profit for INL of about $63 million for the 1998 year, but that is before details of the Sky purchase are known.
They said a 50 percent stake in Sky could cost INL around $300 million, and the funding costs on capital borrowed would be significant.

Robson said once the Sky deal had been sewn up, INL may look to divest its U.S. assets, which include newspapers in Houston and in California. Anlaysts estimate the U.S. assets could fetch in the region of NZ$40 million.
"It's a non-core asset to the group, there's no doubt about that, and we'll probably make a decision about that when we've tied up the Sky thing," Robson said.
He added the company may also look to raise the cover prices on the Saturday editions of its major Wellington daily newspapers The Evening Post and The Dominion.
INL, 49.5 percent owned by Murdoch's News Corp, had no plans to increase the weekday prices, he said.
